title: Docker Containers
subtitle: Lifecycle, configuration and day-to-day operations
description: Go beyond docker run. Understand container state, process behaviour, configuration, port publishing and resource policy.
outcomes: Reason about container lifecycle and exit codes
Configure containers with env, files and secrets
Publish ports safely and set restart/resource policy

lessons.title: The container lifecycle
lessons.summary: Created, running, paused, stopped, removed: what each state means and how to move between them.
objectives: Predict the state after each command
Understand restart policies and exit codes

sections.title: State is derived from the main process
sections.body:
A container is **created** when its filesystem and config exist. It is **running** while PID 1 is alive, **paused** when the freezer cgroup is engaged, and **exited** when PID 1 terminates. It remains in the exited state — with its writable layer and name — until removed.

Restart policies act on exit. `unless-stopped` restarts on failure or daemon restart but respects a manual stop. `always` restarts even after a manual stop when the daemon starts.

sections.caption: The container state machine. Removal is the only irreversible transition.

sections.code:
docker run -d --name app --restart unless-stopped nginx:alpine
docker inspect app --format '{{.State.Status}} pid={{.State.Pid}}'
docker pause app
docker inspect app --format '{{.State.Status}}'
docker unpause app
docker stop app
docker inspect app --format 'status={{.State.Status}} exit={{.State.ExitCode}} oom={{.State.OOMKilled}}'
docker rm app
sections.note: Exit code 0 is success; 137 is SIGKILL/OOM; 143 is SIGTERM. `docker inspect` records OOMKilled explicitly.

exercises.title: State audit
exercises.prompt: Start a container, pause it, stop it, and print status/exit code at each step.
exercises.expected: running → paused → exited with exit code 0 or 143 depending on handler.

exercises.title: OOM investigation
exercises.prompt: Inspect a container and check OOMKilled.

questions.question: A stopped container still exists until…
options: It is removed with docker rm
questions.explain: Stop preserves the container; rm deletes it.

questions.question: Which restart policy respects a manual stop across daemon restarts?
questions.explain: unless-stopped does not restart containers that were explicitly stopped.

lessons.title: run, exec and logs
lessons.summary: The daily trio, including detached mode, interactive mode, TTY allocation and log streaming.
objectives: Choose flags for interactive and detached containers
Use exec without creating a shell dependency
Stream logs without losing the terminal

sections.title: Detached vs interactive
sections.body: `-d` detaches and prints the container ID. `-it` allocates a TTY and keeps stdin open — used for shells and interactive CLIs. `--rm` removes the container on exit. Combining `-d` and `-it` is usually a mistake: a detached container does not need your terminal.

sections.code:
# detached service
docker run -d --name api -p 3000:3000 my-api:1.0

# interactive one-off
docker run --rm -it alpine sh

# run a command in an existing container, without a TTY
docker exec api node -e "console.log(process.version)"

# follow logs, then detach with Ctrl-C (container keeps running)
docker logs -f --tail 100 api

# logs since a timestamp
docker logs --since 10m api

sections.title: Do not build containers that require a TTY
sections.body: A service should log to stdout/stderr and run without stdin. `-it` is for humans, not for production entrypoints.

exercises.title: One-off command
exercises.prompt: Use alpine to print the current date and remove the container afterwards.

exercises.title: Log window
exercises.prompt: Show the last 50 lines from a container and then follow new lines.

questions.question: What does -it do?
options: Allocates a TTY and keeps stdin open
questions.explain: It makes an interactive terminal session.

questions.question: Which command runs a second process in a running container?
questions.explain: exec targets an existing running container.

questions.question: Where should application logs go?
questions.explain: Docker captures stdout/stderr through the configured logging driver.

lessons.title: Ports and publishing
lessons.summary: EXPOSE documents. -p publishes. The distinction prevents a whole class of connectivity bugs.
objectives: Bind published ports to loopback or specific interfaces

sections.title: Two different things
sections.body:
`EXPOSE 3000` in a Dockerfile is documentation: it records intent and is visible in `docker inspect`. It does not make the port reachable from the host. `-p 8080:3000` (or `--publish`) creates a host binding that forwards traffic to the container.

The binding syntax is `[host_ip:]host_port:container_port[/protocol]`. Omitting host_ip binds on all interfaces (`0.0.0.0` and often `::`). Use `127.0.0.1:8080:3000` for local-only services.

sections.code:
docker run -d --name web -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 nginx:alpine
docker port web
docker inspect web --format '{{json .NetworkSettings.Ports}}'

# random host port
docker run -d --name web-random -P nginx:alpine
docker port web-random 80/tcp

sections.title: Port conflicts are a host problem
sections.body: If bind fails with "address already in use", another process or container owns the host port. Find it with `ss -ltnp` or `docker ps --format` and choose a different host port.

exercises.title: Loopback only
exercises.expected: The port is reachable only from the host.

exercises.title: Find the owner
exercises.prompt: A host port is already in use. Find the process listening on it.

questions.question: Does EXPOSE publish a port to the host?
questions.explain: Publishing requires -p or a compose ports entry.

questions.question: Which binding exposes a service only on localhost?
questions.explain: Prefixing the host IP restricts the listener.

questions.question: What does -P do?
options: Publishes all EXPOSEd ports to random host ports
questions.explain: Capital P publishes every exposed port on an ephemeral host port.

lessons.title: Environment, restart policy and resources
lessons.summary: Configure containers without rebuilding, and keep one noisy service from consuming the host.
objectives: Apply CPU, memory and PID limits

sections.title: Configuration at runtime
sections.body:
Environment variables are the simplest configuration channel: `-e KEY=value` or `--env-file .env`. They appear in `docker inspect` and in the process environment, so they are **not** suitable for long-lived secrets. Mount secrets read-only or use Compose secrets for anything sensitive.

Values in the image are defaults; runtime flags override them. Use `docker run --env-file` for grouped settings and keep secrets out of the file.

sections.code:
docker run -d --name api \
  --env-file ./app.env \
  -e LOG_LEVEL=info \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --memory 512m --memory-swap 512m \
  --cpus 1.5 --pids-limit 256 \
  -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 \
  my-api:1.0

docker inspect api --format '{{json .HostConfig.Memory}} {{json .HostConfig.NanoCpus}}'
docker stats --no-stream api
sections.output:
536870912 1500000000
CONTAINER ID   NAME   CPU %   MEM USAGE / LIMIT   MEM %
...             api    0.4%    82.1MiB / 512MiB    16.0%

head: Flag
Effect
rows: Restart on non-zero exit, optionally limited
Always restart, including after daemon start
Like always, but respects manual stop
Hard memory limit (OOM kill beyond it)

sections.title: Memory swap defaults can surprise you
sections.body: Without `--memory-swap`, Docker may allow swap beyond `--memory`. Set both equal for a hard limit, or configure swap deliberately.

exercises.title: Hard limit
exercises.prompt: Run nginx with a 256 MB hard limit and no swap.

exercises.title: Env file
exercises.prompt: Create app.env with APP_PORT=3000 and start a container using it.
exercises.command: printf "APP_PORT=3000\n" > app.env && docker run --rm --env-file app.env alpine env
exercises.expected: Use --env-file app.env and verify with docker exec env.

questions.question: Where should production secrets go?
options: Compose secrets or a mounted secret store
questions.explain: Environment variables are visible in inspect; use secret mechanisms.

questions.question: Which restart policy restarts after a daemon restart but not after a manual stop?
questions.explain: unless-stopped is the practical default for services.

questions.question: A container hits its memory limit. What happens?
options: The kernel OOM killer terminates processes
questions.explain: Cgroup memory limits lead to OOM kills, commonly exit 137.
